explanations.explanation: That's the phrase, friend. Zophar asks, "Should this stream of words go unanswered and such a speaker be vindicated?" (Job 11:2). He's talking about Job's speech, and he treats it like a faucet somebody forgot to turn off. I think Zophar has been holding this one in for a while.

I see how you got here, friend. Job did bring hard words to God, but Zophar calls this something else. He says, "Should this stream of words go unanswered…" (Job 11:2). The phrase he picks is a stream of words.

Job's grief is real, friend. He says, "My groaning comes at the sight of my food" (Job 3:24). Zophar doesn't call it a song, though. He says, "Should this stream of words go unanswered and such a speaker be vindicated?" (Job 11:2). Nobody is humming along over there.

Not quite, baker. Zophar says the opposite. He asks, "Should your babbling put others to silence? Will you scoff without rebuke?" (Job 11:3). Calm and humble would be a very different speech. This one has no soft pillows in it.

Right. Zophar calls Job's words "babbling" and asks, "Will you scoff without rebuke?" (Job 11:3). Those are not words you use for calm and humble. I think if Zophar had a gentle side, it stayed home that day.

Yes, pure. Zophar says, "You have said, ‘My doctrine is sound, and I am pure in Your sight.’" (Job 11:4). He's putting Job's claim right out on the counter for everyone to look at. Whether he's quoting Job exactly is something I'll leave alone, because the text just says Zophar says it.

Job did talk about being weary, and he says, "I loathe my life" (Job 10:1). But Zophar's quote is about something else. He says, "My doctrine is sound, and I am pure in Your sight." (Job 11:4). The word he puts in Job's mouth is pure.

Small would sound pretty humble, and that's not what Zophar is pushing on. He says Job claimed, "My doctrine is sound, and I am pure in Your sight." (Job 11:4). Pure is the word, and it's the one Zophar wants to push back on.

That's it, baker. Zophar says, "Know then that God exacts from you less than your iniquity deserves." (Job 11:6). Iniquity means wrongdoing. Zophar is saying Job is getting off easy, and I think Job did not enjoy hearing that one bit.

explanations.answer: More than he could ever bear
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd go this way, since Job is carrying a lot. But Zophar goes the other direction. He says, "Know then that God exacts from you less than your iniquity deserves." (Job 11:6). So he's saying less, not more.

explanations.answer: Only what he is able to handle
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a comforting line, friend. Zophar doesn't say it, though. He says, "Know then that God exacts from you less than your iniquity deserves." (Job 11:6). It's less than deserved, and it's not a comfort speech.

explanations.answer: Job can't reach those deep things
explanations.explanation: You've got it. Zophar says they are "…higher than the heavens…" and "…deeper than Sheol…" and then asks, "…what can you do?" and "…what can you know?" (Job 11:8). He's using the questions to say Job can't reach them. That's a lot of mountain to climb with a stool and a dream.

explanations.answer: Job should search harder for them
explanations.explanation: I get it, since a question can sound like a challenge to try harder. But Zophar asks, "…what can you do?" and "…what can you know?" (Job 11:8). Those questions are pointing at how far out of reach the deep things are. He doesn't tell Job to dig.

Zophar is heading the other way, baker. He says the deep things are "…higher than the heavens…" and "…deeper than Sheol…" then asks, "…what can you do?" and "…what can you know?" (Job 11:8). The questions are meant to say Job doesn't reach them.
Yes. Zophar asks, "If He comes along to imprison you, or convenes a court, who can stop Him?" (Job 11:10). The question answers itself. Nobody can stop Him.

Not this time, baker. Zophar asks, "If He comes along to imprison you, or convenes a court, who can stop Him?" (Job 11:10). He's asking it so the answer is plain: no one can stop Him. It's a question with no hands raised.
That's right. Zophar says, "Surely He knows the deceit of men. If He sees iniquity, does He not take note?" (Job 11:11). It's another question where the answer is built in. Zophar says He takes note.
Zophar says no such thing. He asks, "If He sees iniquity, does He not take note?" (Job 11:11). So the point is that God does take note. Looking the other way isn't in his question.

explanations.answer: He waits for it to pass
explanations.explanation: That sounds patient, but it's not what Zophar says. He asks, "If He sees iniquity, does He not take note?" (Job 11:11). Taking note is the answer, and waiting for it to pass isn't in there.

Yes, that's his point. Zophar says, "…a witless man can no more become wise than the colt of a wild donkey can be born a man!" (Job 11:12). A donkey colt is not getting born a man, and that's the picture. It's a sharp thing to say, and I think it's aimed at Job.

Zophar means the opposite, friend. He says, "…a witless man can no more become wise than the colt of a wild donkey can be born a man!" (Job 11:12). A wild donkey's colt being born a man isn't happening, so quick learning isn't either.

Time doesn't come into it. Zophar says, "…a witless man can no more become wise than the colt of a wild donkey can be born a man!" (Job 11:12). He's saying it's not going to happen, no matter how long you wait.
That's the one. Zophar says, "…if you put away the iniquity in your hand…" (Job 11:14). It's one more step in his list of ifs. Put it down, and then the speech moves on to what comes after.

explanations.answer: The broken pottery in his hand
explanations.explanation: I like the creativity, baker. But Zophar's list doesn't have pottery in it. He says, "…if you put away the iniquity in your hand…" (Job 11:14). Iniquity is what he wants put away.
A staff is a fair guess for something in a hand. But Zophar says, "…if you put away the iniquity in your hand…" (Job 11:14). It's iniquity he's talking about, and a staff never comes up.

Yes. Zophar says, "…then indeed you will lift up your face without blemish; you will stand firm and unafraid." (Job 11:15). Both pieces are in the same verse. It's a nice picture, even with the sharp talk before it.
Not quite, friend. Right after the without blemish part, Zophar says, "you will stand firm and unafraid." (Job 11:15). So he does say it, and it's in the same verse.

explanations.answer: It will pass and be gone
explanations.explanation: That's it. Zophar says, "…you will forget your misery, recalling it only as waters gone by." (Job 11:16). Water that's gone by doesn't come back around. I think that's the picture he wants Job to see.

explanations.answer: It will return again and again
explanations.explanation: That's a sad picture, and Zophar doesn't paint it. He says, "…you will forget your misery, recalling it only as waters gone by." (Job 11:16). Waters gone by are past, so the misery is the same.

explanations.answer: It will grow deeper over time
explanations.explanation: Zophar says the opposite, baker. He says, "…you will forget your misery, recalling it only as waters gone by." (Job 11:16). Water that has gone by is behind you, not rising.

Not this time, friend. Zophar says, "You will be secure, because there is hope, and you will look around and lie down in safety." (Job 11:18). That's the opposite of never resting easy. Lying down in safety is a pretty good rest.
That's right. Zophar says, "…you will look around and lie down in safety." (Job 11:18). He never says Job will go without rest. In fact he says he'll be secure.
Yes, court. Zophar says, "You will lie down without fear, and many will court your favor." (Job 11:19). To court someone's favor is to go looking for it. I bet that's a lot of attention.
Lose is an easy one to guess when things have gone badly. But Zophar says, "…many will court your favor." (Job 11:19). The word is court, and it means people seeking his favor.
I see why scorn comes to mind, baker. It isn't what Zophar says, though. He says, "…many will court your favor." (Job 11:19). Courting favor is the opposite of scorn.

That's right. Zophar says, "But the eyes of the wicked will fail, and escape will elude them; they will hope for their last breath." (Job 11:20). It's a heavy way to end, and I think it's meant to sit hard. Zophar is putting it right beside his picture of Job's bright future.
That sounds hopeful, friend, and it's not in the verse. Zophar says, "…escape will elude them; they will hope for their last breath." (Job 11:20). It's a heavy line, and a second chance isn't in it.
It's the other way around, baker. Zophar says, "…escape will elude them; they will hope for their last breath." (Job 11:20). That's a hard line, and a long life isn't what they're hoping for.
